 1              III.   FORECASTED PLANT BALANCES AND PLANT
 2                              RELATED EXPENSES

 3   Q.   Are you involved in the development of net plant balances used to determine

 4        the Base Period and Future Test Year rate bases?

 5   A.   Yes. Capital Asset Accounting is responsible for all aspects of the fixed asset

 6        accounting for SPS. Based on historical plant balances and the capital expenditure

 7        forecasts prepared by each business area, Capital Asset Accounting has developed

 8        and provided the information regarding forecasted plant balances and plant-related

 9        information that has been used in the rate base and revenue requirement analyses

10        presented by Ms. Johnson in her pre-filed direct testimony.

11   Q.   Please explain what you mean by forecasted plant balances and plant-related

12        expenses.

13   A.   Those terms refer to the development of the plant balance rolled forward from the

14        last month of the Base Period through the forecasted Future Test Year Period, along

15        with the calculation of all associated plant‑related expenses. Plant-related expenses

16        included in this roll-forward are book depreciation, tax depreciation and

17        deductions, and annual deferred taxes. Besides plant balances, accumulated book

18        depreciation and accumulated deferred tax balances are forecasted in conjunction

19        with the calculation of the plant-related expenses. Attachment MAK-2 takes the

                                               8
                                      Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                       Direct Testimony
                                               of
                                      Michele A. Kietzman

 1        capital expenditures for the installation of new assets forecasted by the business

 2        areas and converts them into plant additions. These additions to plant are among

 3        the main components that influence changes in rate base and, thus, the revenue

 4        requirement.

 5   Q.   What standards does SPS use to establish its net plant balance?

 6   A.   To establish the net plant balance, SPS follows the applicable accounting rules

 7        established by Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (“GAAP”), the Uniform

 8        System of Accounts (“USOA”) established by the Federal Energy Regulatory

 9        Commission (“FERC”) for public utilities, and the internal policies and guidelines

10        established by XES’s Capital Asset Accounting Department. Commission rules

11        require that SPS maintain its books and records in compliance with the USOA. 2

12   Q.   How do plant additions affect rate base?

13   A.   Insofar as plant is concerned, rate base has two main components: the plant-in-

14        service balance and the accumulated-provision-for-depreciation balance. Plant

15        additions increase the gross plant in-service component of rate base. Conversely,

16        annual depreciation expense is added to the accumulated provision for depreciation,

17        which reduces rate base. If plant additions were equal to depreciation expense in a


          2
              17.3.510.10(A) NMAC.

                                               9
                                      Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                       Direct Testimony
                                               of
                                      Michele A. Kietzman

 1        given year, the plant-related rate base would remain constant. If plant-related rate

 2        base increases from one year to the next, it is because plant additions exceed the

 3        depreciation expense.

 4   Q.   Are the additions to rate base typically equal to the capital expenditures in a

 5        given year?

 6   A.   No. The changes to plant rate base for a given year reflect the original cost of assets

 7        placed in service during that year, regardless of when the utility spent the capital to

 8        construct or acquire the assets. In contrast, capital expenditures during a given year

 9        include the outlays for capital projects during that year, including amounts spent

10        for Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”) and Removal Work in Progress

11        (“RWIP”). For example, capital expended in 2024 for an asset placed in service in

12        2025 would be classified as capital expenditures in 2024 but would not become a

13        plant addition and enter rate base until 2025.

14   Q.   Please describe what you mean when you refer to CWIP and RWIP.

15   A.   CWIP is an account used to gather all construction-related costs together as those

16        costs are incurred during the construction of an asset.         During construction,

17        Allowance for Funds Used During Construction (“AFUDC”) is added to CWIP,

18        unless a current return on CWIP is permitted. The accumulation of the construction

19        expenditures and AFUDC continues until the asset is used and useful, which is

                                                10
                                    Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                    Michele A. Kietzman

 1        typically when the asset is placed into service. At that time, the accumulated

 2        balance is transferred from the accumulated CWIP balance to the plant-in-service

 3        balance. In short, CWIP expenditures are for future assets that will become plant

 4        additions on the in-service date of the project. RWIP expenditures are for the

 5        removal of assets and are recorded as accumulated depreciation when the costs

 6        occur.

 7   Q.   Is CWIP part of SPS’s Base Period, Linkage Data Timeframe or Future Test

 8        Year rate base in this case?

 9   A.   No. Amounts are not included in rate base until the asset is fully constructed and

10        closed to plant in-service, at which time the balance ceases to be classified as

11        CWIP. When an asset is placed in service and thereby deemed used and useful, the

12        accumulation of construction charges is closed to plant in-service, FERC Account

13        106, Construction Completed Not Classified (a holding account once the asset is in

14        use but not yet unitized) and FERC Account 101, Electric Plant in-Service (the

15        account where the asset is recorded when unitized).

16   Q.   If CWIP is not included in rate base, why are you discussing it in your

17        testimony?

18   A.   CWIP is the basis for developing all plant balances and plant-related information

19        in this case. The process of moving a construction project from CWIP to plant in-

                                              11
                                             Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                              Direct Testimony
                                                      of
                                             Michele A. Kietzman

 1           service based on the project’s in-service date produces the plant additions that then

 2           form the basis from which all other plant-related information can be derived. Stated

 3           otherwise, even though CWIP is not a component of rate base or the revenue

 4           requirement in this case, it is necessary to show the development of CWIP balances

 5           because they are instrumental in determining plant additions. 3

 6   Q.      Please describe how closings to plant-in-service are determined.

 7   A.      For projects with an individually assigned work order, closings to plant-in-service

 8           are determined based on the actual in-service date on the work order. At the in-

 9           service date, the accumulated CWIP expenditures for the project are moved to plant

10           in-service, accrual of AFUDC is stopped, and book depreciation begins. Typically,

11           charges can continue for a short period after the in-service date on a project. These

12           charges are for recognition of the final bills from vendors, testing of the equipment,

13           restoration of the ground, settlement of any disputes, and returning unused stock to

14           inventory.

15                    For work orders that are routinely completed, such as the extension of

16           service to new customers, SPS typically closes them on a monthly or quarterly



             3
               After a project is closed to plant in service, the AFUDC that had been accrued while the project
     was recorded as CWIP becomes part of the gross plant balance.

                                                        12

 1        basis. These workorders are highly standardized and are typically completed in

 2        days or a few weeks, as opposed to months or years for discrete projects. Thus, for

 3        example, all routine work completed during a month may be closed to plant-in-

 4        service on the last day of that month.

 5   Q.   Please describe the development of Future Test Year plant and plant-related

 6        information.

 7   A.   The most recent five-year forecast information approved in July 2025 served as the

 8        basis of the forecasted plant and plant-related information used in this rate case.

 9        The Base Period is composed of 12 months of actual information. The Linkage

10        Data rolls forward the plant information from June 30, 2025 to the first month of

11        the Future Test Year. For the Future Test Year, the rate base is developed from a

12        13-month average of the monthly ending plant balances. As with any plant

13        information, the forecasted balances are influenced by the activity in the preceding

14        years. Therefore, the plant information is rolled forward month‑by‑month (known

15        as a “monthly roll forward”). Forecasted plant and plant-related balances are built

16        upon the actuals using the forecasted changes in plant and plant-related expenses

17        until all months have been calculated through the end of the Future Test Year.

18        Attachment MAK-2 summarizes this roll forward calculation from July 1, 2024

 1        through November 30, 2027. This roll forward serves as the basis for the Future

 2        Test Year plant-in-service balances used by Ms. Johnson in the determination of

 3        the Future Test Year rate base. Attachment MAK-10 provides a numerical link of

 4        plant-related data between my roll forward and the revenue requirement study (total

 5        company) numbers contained in Ms. Johnson’s Attachment AMJ-6.

 6   Q.   What are the main components of plant and plant-related information

 7        provided in the roll forward?

 8   A.   Plant and plant-related information consists of several components. The three most

 9        influential components are CWIP, plant-in-service, and the accumulated provision

10        for depreciation.

16        at a cost element level that provides estimated breakout between material, labor,

17        outside services and similar classifications of costs. SPS does not forecast cost

18        elements, so cost elements for the Linkage Data and the Future Test Year are

 1                 IV.     DETERMINATION OF FERC ACCOUNTS

 2   Q.   How are FERC Accounts determined for the Linkage Data and the Future

 3        Test Year?

 4   A.   FERC functions, such as transmission, are assigned during the forecast process

 5        based on the attributes of the overall construction project. Similar to elements of

 6        cost, costs are then assigned to individual, more detailed FERC Accounts based on

 7        historical percentages for each type of plant derived from actual work for the

 8        defined function in the Base Period.

 9   Q.   Has FERC recently issued an order that requires changes in FERC accounts

10        for certain types of assets?

11   A.   Yes. FERC Order No. 898 was effective January 1, 2025, modifying the USOA,

12        as further discussed in Section X, FERC Order No. 898.

 1        V.       SPS’S PROPOSED TREATMENT OF LEGACY ELECTRIC
 2                              DISTRIBUTION METERS

 3   Q.        Please provide background related to legacy meters recovery.

 4   A.        SPS is in the process of replacing its legacy Automated Meter Reading (“AMR”)

 5             meters or “legacy meters” with Advanced Metering Infrastructure (“AMI”) meters.

 6             My testimony proposes a recovery mechanism for SPS’s capital investment in the

 7             legacy meters that will be retired prior to being fully depreciated at the time of

 8             concluding AMI deployment. It is reasonable for SPS to recover all prudent,

 9             previously authorized capital investments, such as the legacy AMR meters.

10   Q.        Are the costs for both the legacy AMR meters and new AMI meters readily

11             identifiable on SPS’s books?

12   A.        Yes, SPS has already isolated the meters into dedicated FERC sub-accounts, further

13             segregated by state, which allows the new AMI meters to be capitalized and

14             depreciated entirely separate from the legacy meters that are being retired and

15             ensures only the costs attributable to New Mexico legacy meters are included in the

16             proposed regulatory asset.

 1   Q.   Has SPS completed the installation of the New Mexico AMI meters at the time

 2        of this filing?

 3   A.   No. SPS currently projects that all New Mexico AMI meter installations will be

 4        completed by March 2026.

 5   Q.   What regulatory authorizations are required to establish this type of

 6        regulatory asset?

 7   A.   To support the establishment of a regulatory asset and future amortization of these

 8        costs, SPS would need an Order from the Commission that:

 9            1) authorizes the transfer of the net unrecovered legacy meter costs to a

11            2) approves the amortization period for this regulatory asset, which would be

15   A.   Yes. In Case No. 22-00178-UT, SPS requested that the Commission authorize it

 1   Q.      What was the outcome of that filing?

 2   A.      The commission ordered as follows, “The Commission hereby approves of SPS’

 3           recovery of the undepreciated balance of legacy meters that have been removed

 4           from service but does not approve of a return on that asset. The undepreciated

 5           balance of legacy meters removed from service shall be removed from the rate base

 6           in the next rate case, and placed into a regulatory asset that earns no interest. The

 7           recovery period of this asset will be decided in the Company’s next rate case, but

 8           in no event will the amortization period be longer than ten years.” 4

 9   Q.      How does SPS propose to recover its remaining investment in the legacy

 5   Q.   How is the proration calculated in general?

 6   A.   The proration calculation takes the monthly deferred tax amounts and applies a

 7        proration factor to it. The proration factor for a month is the number of days

 8        remaining in the year for that month divided by the total number of days in the year.

 9        To determine the remaining days for a month, one starts with the first month for the

10        period being prorated and the number of days in that month. This number of days

11        is subtracted from the total days in the year to get the remaining days in the year

12        for that month, then adding one day for the last day of the month. For the second

13        month, the sum of days in the first two months is subtracted from the total days in

14        a year, again adding one day for the last day in the second month. This continues

15        for each month until one gets to the last month which has one day remaining.

16               For example, if all 12 months in a year are being prorated, the total number

17        of days in a non-leap year is 365 days. If January is the first month being prorated,

18        the remaining days for January are calculated by taking the number of days in the
